beginner: Corn grows best in deep, rich, well-drained soil like loam. Because it grows tall and feeds heavily, mixing in compost before planting helps the soil hold the steady moisture the plants need when the ears are forming.
seasoned: Deep, fertile, well-drained loam suits corn best. Its roots run deep and it feeds heavily, so a soil rich in organic matter that holds moisture through the tasseling and silking window without waterlogging gives the fullest ears.

beginner: Both sandy and clay-based soils can grow corn as long as they drain well. Sandy soil warms up early but dries out and loses fertilizer faster, so water and feed a little more often. Heavier soil holds food longer but should be loosened so it does not form a hard crust over the seeds.
seasoned: Sandy and clay loams both grow good corn if drainage is sound. Sandy beds warm faster and suit early sowings but dry out and leach nitrogen quicker, so they need more frequent water and sidedressing; heavier soils hold feeding longer but must be worked so they do not crust over the seed.

beginner: Stay away from cold, soggy, poorly drained soil. Corn seed sits and rots in cold, wet ground instead of sprouting, and standing water keeps the roots from feeding, which corn needs to do a lot of.
seasoned: Avoid cold, wet, poorly drained ground. Corn seed rots or suffers chilling injury when sown into soil below 60°F, and standing water stunts the shallow feeder roots and starves the plant of the nitrogen it needs.

beginner: Corn likes deep, rich, well-drained soil. If water pools on your bed after rain, work in compost and consider a raised bed so the roots never sit wet.
seasoned: Deep, fertile, well-drained loam with compost worked in before planting. The load-bearing traits are warmth at sowing and steady moisture with high fertility through tasseling and silking.

beginner: Corn does best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, around a pH of 6.0 to 6.8. Most garden beds are already close; a soil test is the only way to know for sure and to catch soil that is too acidic.
seasoned: A soil pH of 6.0 to 6.8 suits field corn. Lime an acidic bed to reach that range the season before, and confirm both pH and fertility with a soil test, since corn's heavy feeding rewards a well-limed, well-fed bed.

beginner: Corn is hungry, especially for nitrogen. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil at planting, then feed again when the plants are about knee-high and once more when the tassels appear at the top. Those are the times corn needs the most food. In sandy soil or after heavy rain, feed a little more often, since the nitrogen washes away.
seasoned: Corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder. Work a balanced starter into the bed at planting, then sidedress nitrogen twice: once when plants are knee-high and again as the tassels form, the two windows when demand peaks. Sandy soils and heavy rain leach nitrogen, so split the sidedressing further where that applies.

beginner: Time to feed your corn. It is about knee-high now, which is when it needs a nitrogen boost.
seasoned: Sidedress nitrogen now: your corn is at the knee-high stage where demand climbs steeply.

beginner: Corn wants plenty of nitrogen. Use a balanced fertilizer at planting, then feed nitrogen again as it grows.
seasoned: Nitrogen-forward feeding: a balanced starter, then nitrogen sidedressings at knee-high and tasseling.

beginner: Use the amount on the fertilizer label for a hungry vegetable, then two lighter nitrogen feedings as it grows.
seasoned: Follow the label rate for a heavy-feeding vegetable; a common approach is a balanced starter plus two nitrogen sidedressings.

beginner: Corn is the tall centerpiece of the classic Three Sisters planting with beans and squash. The beans feed the soil the corn is so hungry for, and the squash shades the ground below. Keep corn away from tomatoes, since the two share the same ear-and-fruit worm.
seasoned: Corn anchors the traditional Three Sisters trio: beans climb it and fix nitrogen for its heavy demand, and squash sprawls below as a living mulch. The main caution is tomatoes, which share the pest Helicoverpa zea (corn earworm / tomato fruitworm), so a shared planting can concentrate it.

beginner: The Three Sisters partner: beans pull nitrogen from the air and enrich the soil for hungry corn, and can climb the stalks.
seasoned: Pole beans use the cornstalk as a living trellis and fix nitrogen that offsets corn's heavy demand; the pairing is the well-documented Three Sisters polyculture. The benefit is soil-and-structure rather than a measured pest effect.

beginner: The third Sister: its big sprawling leaves shade the soil around the corn, holding moisture and smothering weeds.
seasoned: Squash rounds out the trio as a ground-covering living mulch that shades soil, conserves moisture, and suppresses weeds around the corn. A soil-and-space benefit; give it room so it does not swamp young corn.

beginner: Corn and tomatoes are hit by the same worm, called the corn earworm on corn and the tomato fruitworm on tomatoes, so growing them together can build it up.
seasoned: Corn and tomato share Helicoverpa zea (corn earworm on corn, tomato fruitworm on tomato). Interplanting gives the pest two sequential hosts in one spot, so separating them limits the buildup.

beginner: A fat, striped caterpillar tunneling into the tip of the ear under the husk, leaving chewed kernels and dark droppings. It usually stays near the tip, but the damage can let mold in.
seasoned: Chewed, frass-fouled kernels at the ear tip where a fat, striped caterpillar has fed under the husk; silks may be clipped, and tip damage opens the door to mold.

beginner: The corn earworm, a caterpillar whose moth lays eggs on the silks. The young caterpillars crawl down the silks into the ear. It is the same pest as the tomato fruitworm.
seasoned: The corn earworm (Helicoverpa zea), whose moths lay eggs on fresh silks; the hatching larvae follow the silks down into the ear tip. It is the same species as the tomato fruitworm.

beginner: The good news is the worm usually stays at the very tip, so you can just cut that part off. A classic trick is a few drops of vegetable or mineral oil on the silks after they have been pollinated, and an organic spray such as Bt or spinosad works if you time it to fresh silks.
seasoned: Because most feeding is confined to the ear tip, the loss is often cosmetic: cut off the damaged tip at the kitchen. A few drops of mineral oil applied to the silk channel after pollination is a traditional home tactic; a spinosad or Bt product timed to fresh silks is the labeled organic option.

beginner: Pick varieties with long, tight husks that make it harder for the worm to get in, and plant early so the ears silk before the moths are at their worst in late summer.
seasoned: Choose varieties with tight, long husk cover, which slows the larvae, and plant early so the crop silks before peak moth flights in late summer.

beginner: Tiny holes in the young leaves, then sawdust-like droppings where the leaves meet the stalk, and small holes bored into the stalk itself. Badly tunneled stalks can break.
seasoned: Small shot-hole feeding in the whorl leaves, then sawdust-like frass at leaf axils and pin-sized entry holes in the stalk and ear shank; tunneled stalks weaken and can snap.

beginner: The European corn borer, a caterpillar that starts by chewing the young leaves, then tunnels into the stalks, hollowing them out.
seasoned: The European corn borer (Ostrinia nubilalis), a caterpillar that first feeds in the leaf whorl, then bores into stalks and ear shanks, weakening the plant from inside.

beginner: Check the young leaf whorls and rub out the egg patches and small caterpillars before they tunnel in. An organic Bt spray only works while they are still out on the leaves; once inside the stalk you cannot reach them.
seasoned: Scout the whorls and pick off egg masses and young larvae before they bore in; a Bt product reaches them only while they are still feeding in the open whorl. Once inside the stalk they are protected.

beginner: Chop up and dig in the old cornstalks after harvest, because the borer spends the winter inside them, and move your corn to a new spot each year.
seasoned: Shred and turn under cornstalks after harvest, since the borer overwinters in old stalks; rotating away from last year's patch helps too.

beginner: Young corn plants cut off right at the ground overnight, as if with scissors. If you dig near a cut plant, you often find a fat gray caterpillar curled up in the soil.
seasoned: Young seedlings clipped off at or just above the soil line overnight, often toppled and left; a gray, greasy-looking caterpillar curls up just below the surface nearby.

beginner: Cutworms, fat caterpillars that live in the soil and come out at night to chew through young stems at the base.
seasoned: Cutworms, the soil-dwelling larvae of several night-flying moths, which sever tender seedling stems at the base as they feed after dark.

beginner: Go out at night with a flashlight and pick them off, or dig around a freshly cut plant to find the culprit. A little collar of cardboard or foil pushed into the soil around each stem keeps them out.
seasoned: Handpick at night or just under the soil around fresh damage; a cardboard or foil collar pushed an inch into the soil around each seedling blocks them.

beginner: Clear weeds from the bed before you plant, because the moths lay their eggs in weedy soil, and plant into warm soil so the seedlings grow quickly past the tender stage.
seasoned: Keep the bed weed-free before planting, since cutworm moths lay in weedy ground, and delay sowing until the soil is warm and seedlings grow fast through the vulnerable stage.

beginner: Tiny dark beetles that hop away when you get close, leaving the young leaves peppered with little pinholes. Bad early damage stunts small plants and can spread a corn disease.
seasoned: Tiny dark beetles that jump when disturbed, leaving fine pinholes and shot-hole pitting in the leaves of young plants; heavy early feeding stunts seedlings and can transmit Stewart's wilt.

beginner: Small beetles called flea beetles that chew young corn leaves. One kind also carries the germ that causes Stewart's wilt, a corn disease, spreading it as it feeds.
seasoned: Several flea beetle species that feed on corn seedlings; the corn flea beetle also carries the bacterium that causes Stewart's wilt from plant to plant.

beginner: Small plants usually grow past light damage. If the beetles are thick, cover the young plants with a lightweight row cover, taking it off when the tassels form so the wind can pollinate, and use an organic spinosad spray only if you must.
seasoned: Seedlings usually outgrow light feeding; where beetles are thick, a floating row cover over young plants (removed at tasseling for pollination) protects them, and spinosad is labeled if needed.

beginner: Pull weeds that shelter the beetles, plant into warm soil so the corn grows quickly, and pick varieties that resist Stewart's wilt if it is a problem where you live.
seasoned: Control weeds that harbor the beetles, plant after the soil warms so seedlings grow fast, and choose Stewart's-wilt-tolerant varieties where the disease occurs.

beginner: Ears torn open and eaten, and stalks knocked over, appearing overnight right when the corn is ready. Raccoons seem to know the exact night before you plan to harvest.
seasoned: Ears pulled down, husked, and half-eaten overnight as the kernels fill, with stalks knocked flat; the damage can arrive fast once the ears are worth raiding.

beginner: Raccoons, which raid ripe corn at night and can clear a small patch in a night or two. They are one of the most common reasons a home corn crop is lost.
seasoned: Raccoons, which raid corn from the milk and dough stages on and can strip a patch in a night or two; they are one of the most common causes of a lost home crop.

beginner: You cannot spray for raccoons; you have to keep them out. A short two-wire electric fence, switched on as the ears get close to ready, is the surest way to protect the patch.
seasoned: There is no spray; exclusion is the answer. A two-wire electric fence (about 4 and 8 inches high) turned on as ears near maturity is the most reliable home defense.

beginner: Set up and turn on the fence before the corn is ripe, not after the first raid. Once raccoons find your corn, they come back every night.
seasoned: Put the fence up and energize it before the ears fill out, not after the first raid, since once raccoons find the patch they return nightly.

beginner: Puffy silver-white growths on the ears or stalks that later burst into a cloud of black powder. On the ear, these galls take the place of kernels. They show up most on stressed or damaged plants.
seasoned: Silvery-white galls on ears, tassels, or stalks that swell, then rupture to release a mass of powdery black spores; ear galls replace kernels and are most common on stressed or injured plants.

beginner: A fungus that gets in through wounds and silks, especially in hot, dry spells, and forms the galls. Its spores can survive in the soil for years.
seasoned: The fungus Ustilago maydis, which enters through wounds and silks and is favored by hot, dry weather punctuated by injury; its spores survive years in the soil.

beginner: There is no home spray. Cut off and throw away (do not compost) the galls before they burst, so their spores do not spread into your soil.
seasoned: There is no spray for the home garden; cut off and bag the galls before they rupture and blacken, to keep spores out of the soil. Do not compost them.

beginner: Try not to injure the plants while weeding, keep water and feeding steady so the corn is not stressed, move your corn each year, and pick more resistant varieties if smut keeps coming back.
seasoned: Avoid wounding plants during cultivation, keep moisture and fertility steady to reduce stress, rotate away from infected beds, and choose more tolerant varieties where smut recurs.

beginner: Small rusty-brown, powdery spots on both sides of the leaves that darken later in the season. A bad case yellows the leaves and can leave the ears less full.
seasoned: Small cinnamon-brown, powdery pustules scattered on both leaf surfaces, darkening toward the season's end; heavy infection yellows and kills leaf tissue and can cut ear fill.

beginner: A fungus whose spores blow in on the wind and take hold in cool, damp weather. In most gardens it arrives fresh each year rather than surviving the winter in place.
seasoned: The fungus Puccinia sorghi, whose spores blow in on the wind and infect under cool, moist, humid conditions; it does not overwinter in most northern gardens but arrives each year on wind currents.

beginner: Most gardens can live with a little rust. Pull off the worst lower leaves to slow it and give the plants air. You rarely need to spray in a home garden.
seasoned: Most home crops tolerate rust without treatment; remove badly infected lower leaves to slow spread and improve airflow. A labeled fungicide is rarely needed in a garden.

beginner: Pick rust-resistant varieties, which are easy to find, and plant early so the corn is nearly done before rust gets bad late in summer. Water at the base when you can.
seasoned: Choose rust-resistant hybrids, which are widely available, and plant early so the crop matures before rust builds late in the season; avoid overhead watering where practical.

beginner: Long yellow streaks with wavy edges running down the leaves, appearing after flea beetles have been feeding. A bad early case wilts and stunts young plants and can kill them.
seasoned: Long, pale-green to yellow streaks with wavy margins running along the leaves, following flea-beetle feeding scars; severe early infection wilts and stunts seedlings, sometimes killing them.

beginner: A bacterium spread by the corn flea beetle as it feeds. After a mild winter more beetles survive, so the disease tends to be worse the next year.
seasoned: The bacterium Pantoea stewartii, carried and introduced by the corn flea beetle; mild winters that let more beetles survive drive worse outbreaks the following year.

beginner: You cannot cure an infected plant; pull and throw away badly affected seedlings. The real control is keeping the flea beetles that spread it in check.
seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy severely affected seedlings. Management is aimed at the flea-beetle vector, not the bacterium itself.

beginner: Grow resistant varieties, which is the main defense, and keep flea beetles off young plants with a row cover or an organic treatment so they cannot pass the disease along.
seasoned: Grow resistant or tolerant hybrids, the primary defense, and manage flea beetles on young plants with row cover or a labeled treatment to break the transmission cycle.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist. Pay the closest attention from the time the tassels appear through when the ears are filling out, which is when corn needs water the most.
seasoned: Water regularly to keep the root zone evenly moist through the season, with the highest demand from tasseling through silking and ear fill.

beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, and closer to 1.5 inches while the corn is pollinating and filling ears. Water deeply so it soaks down to the roots rather than just wetting the surface.
seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week from rain and irrigation, rising toward 1.5 inches per week across the pollination and ear-fill window; water deeply to wet the full root zone.

beginner: Give corn a deep soak rather than frequent light sprinkles. Corn handles overhead watering better than many crops, but watering at the base wastes less and keeps the leaves drier.
seasoned: Deep soaking at intervals suits corn. Overhead watering is tolerated far better than on disease-prone crops, but soaker or furrow watering conserves water and keeps the canopy from staying wet.

beginner: If the soil stays soggy and the lower leaves yellow while the plant stalls, the roots are drowning. Ease off and let it drain.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and stunted, stalled growth in ground that stays wet point to waterlogged, oxygen-starved roots.

beginner: Leaves that roll up like tubes in the afternoon mean the corn is too dry. If this happens while the tassels and silks are out, you get ears with missing kernels, so keep the water steady then.
seasoned: Leaves that roll or curl at midday, especially near tasseling, signal drought stress; stress in the silking window desiccates silks and pollen and leaves gappy, poorly filled ears.

beginner: Keep the seedbed evenly damp, not soggy, until the seedlings come up. Cold, wet soil rots the seed before it sprouts.
seasoned: Sown into warm soil, corn wants an evenly moist seedbed until emergence, but not saturated: cold, waterlogged soil rots the seed.

beginner: Water the young plants evenly as they get their roots down.
seasoned: Grow young plants on with steady, even moisture while the root system establishes.

beginner: Give about 1 inch of water a week as the plants shoot up, and water deeply so it reaches the growing roots.
seasoned: Water use climbs steadily as the plants gain height; keep about 1 inch per week and water deeply to follow the deepening roots.

beginner: When the tassels are shedding pollen, the corn must not dry out. Dry soil now means poorly filled ears later, so keep the water steady and generous.
seasoned: Tasseling opens the critical-moisture window: water stress now, as pollen sheds, cuts pollen viability and the eventual kernel set. Keep moisture high and steady.

beginner: Silking is the most important time of all for water. If the plants get dry now, the silks cannot do their job and the ears come out with gaps, so water deeply and keep it up.
seasoned: Silking is the single most moisture-sensitive stage: drought desiccates the silks and drops pollination, giving blank tips and gappy ears. This is where steady water pays off most.

beginner: Keep watering steadily while the kernels plump up, since letting it dry now costs you kernels at the tip. As the crop nears the end, ease off so the grain can start to harden and dry.
seasoned: Demand stays high as the kernels fill; stress here aborts kernels at the ear tip. Hold steady moisture through the fill, then ease off as the crop nears maturity so the grain can begin to dry.

beginner: Cut back and then stop watering as the corn nears the end, so the ears can dry out on the plant. Field corn is picked dry and hard, not soft and juicy, so you want it to dry down at the finish.
seasoned: Ease off and then stop watering as the crop nears maturity so the grain can dry down on the stalk. Field corn is harvested dry and hard, not at a plump milk stage, so a dry finish is what you want.

beginner: The most important time to keep water steady is when the tassels and silks are out and the ears are filling.
seasoned: The critical moisture window is tasseling through silking and into ear fill; do not let the bed dry out then.

seasoned: Tasseling, silking, and ear fill are the moisture-critical stages; drought at silking is the single most damaging, giving gappy, poorly filled ears.

beginner: You do not need to harden off corn. It is planted straight into the garden from seed.
seasoned: Not applicable. Field corn is direct-sown in place and is not started indoors or hardened off.

beginner: Plant corn seeds right where they will grow, once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F and frost is past. Corn does not like having its roots disturbed and comes up fast anyway, so there is little reason to start it indoors.
seasoned: Direct-sow into warm soil (at least 60°F) after the last spring frost. Corn resents root disturbance and germinates quickly in place, so transplanting offers little gain and risks setting plants back.

beginner: Once the kernels are fully dry and shelled off the cob, field corn keeps like any dry grain. Store it in a sealed jar somewhere cool and dry. Make sure it is thoroughly dry first, or it can mold in storage.
seasoned: Fully dried, shelled field corn is a dry grain and stores at room temperature. Keep the shelled kernels in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place once they reach about 13 to 15 percent moisture; grain that is not fully dry will mold or attract insects.

beginner: You do not need to refrigerate dry corn, but putting the shelled kernels in the fridge or freezer for a few days first is a good way to kill any tiny insects before you store it.
seasoned: Refrigeration is not needed for dry grain, but chilling or freezing the shelled kernels for a few days is a simple way to kill any weevils or grain-moth eggs before long-term storage.

beginner: The freezer is the best place to keep shelled corn for a long time. It stays good and stays bug-free. Grind it into cornmeal only when you need it, because whole kernels last much longer than ground meal.
seasoned: For long keeping, store shelled, fully dry kernels in the freezer, which preserves quality and prevents insect damage. Grind to meal only as needed, since whole grain keeps far longer than ground meal.

beginner: Field corn is kept as a dry grain rather than eaten fresh. The main thing is to dry the kernels thoroughly, then keep them dry and free of insects. Whole dry kernels last for years in a cool or frozen spot, but once you grind them into cornmeal, use it within a few months.
seasoned: Field corn is stored as dry grain, not eaten fresh. The whole task is getting the kernels fully dry (about 13 to 15 percent moisture) and keeping them dry and insect-free. Whole kernels stored cold or frozen keep for years, while ground cornmeal is best used within a few months.

beginner: There are two broad choices. Old open-pollinated heirlooms like John Haulk, Cocke's Prolific, or Reid's Yellow Dent are tall, full of character, and let you save your own seed, but they can top 10 feet and take a long season. Modern grain hybrids are shorter, faster, and more even, though you cannot save their seed. Either way, keep field corn well away from sweet corn and popcorn, because its pollen will spoil them.
seasoned: Field-corn choice splits between tall open-pollinated heirlooms (John Haulk, Cocke's Prolific, and classics like Reid's Yellow Dent or Bloody Butcher), prized for flavor and seed-saving but 10 feet or more tall and full-season, and compact modern grain hybrids picked by relative maturity for a shorter, more uniform, better-standing crop. Whichever you grow, keep it isolated from sweet corn and popcorn, since its pollen ruins both.

beginner: If you plant the seeds close together to be sure they come up, thin them to about 8 to 12 inches apart within the block when they are a few inches tall. Cut the extra seedlings off at the ground instead of pulling them, so you do not disturb the roots of the ones you are keeping.
seasoned: If you sow thickly to insure a stand, thin within the block to a final in-row spacing of 8 to 12 inches once seedlings are a few inches tall. Snip the extras at the soil line rather than pulling, to spare the shallow roots of the plants you keep.

beginner: Field corn is not suited to pots. It grows tall, feeds heavily, and must be planted in a block of several plants for wind pollination, so it belongs in a garden bed, not a container.
seasoned: Field corn is a poor container crop: it is tall and hungry and depends on a block planting for wind pollination, none of which a single pot supports. Grow it in the ground.

beginner: Not applicable. Corn is grown in garden beds, not in self-watering pots.

beginner: Try not to plant corn in the same spot two years running. Moving it each year keeps corn diseases and pests from building up and gives the soil a rest from its heavy feeding.
seasoned: Avoid following corn with corn in the same bed; rotating breaks the buildup of soil-borne diseases and corn pests, and spreads out the crop's heavy nitrogen demand.

beginner: Move your corn to a new spot each year, on about a two-to-three-year cycle. Planting it where beans or peas grew the year before gives it the extra nitrogen it wants.
seasoned: Rotate corn on a two-to-three-year cycle and place it after a nitrogen-fixing legume where you can, since corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder.

beginner: Plant the seeds about 1 to 2 inches deep once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F, laying out a block of short rows rather than one long row. Keep the bed evenly damp but not soggy, since cold, wet soil rots the seed.
seasoned: Sow about 1 to 2 inches deep once soil is at least 60°F, into a block of short rows. Keep the seedbed evenly moist but not saturated; cold, wet soil rots the seed.

beginner: Bare soil for about a week, then a pointed shoot pushes up and the first leaf opens. Corn comes up in about 4 to 7 days in warm soil, slower when it is cool.
seasoned: Bare soil for roughly a week, then the coleoptile spikes through and the first blade unfurls. Emergence takes about 4 to 7 days in warm soil and much longer in cool soil.

beginner: Have your corn come up yet? Write down the date you first saw the seedlings break the soil.
seasoned: Have your corn seedlings emerged? Note the date to track real days from sowing rather than the seed-packet estimate.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and pull weeds early, since small corn does not compete well with them. Weed shallowly to protect the roots near the surface. If you planted thickly, thin to about 8 to 12 inches apart now.
seasoned: Keep the block evenly moist and weed-free; young corn competes poorly with weeds. Cultivate shallowly to spare the surface roots. Thin now to a final 8 to 12 inches in the row if you sowed thickly.

beginner: The young plants send up several long, narrow leaves and reach a few inches tall by two or three weeks. This is when flea beetles and cutworms can do the most damage, so watch for tiny holes and cut-off stems.
seasoned: The seedlings put out a few strap-shaped leaves and stand a few inches tall by around two to three weeks. This is the stage flea beetles and cutworms do the most harm, so watch for pinholes and clipped stems.

beginner: How do your young corn plants look? Note any bare patches, thinning, or chewed leaves.
seasoned: How is your corn stand looking? Note any gaps, thinning you did, or early insect damage.

beginner: Feed with nitrogen when the plants are about knee-high, and keep the water steady as they shoot up. Pull a little soil around the bases to steady the tall stalks, and avoid injuring them, which can let in disease.
seasoned: Sidedress nitrogen at knee-high and keep moisture steady as the plants stretch up. Hill a little soil around the base for support, and hold off overhead work that could injure stalks and invite smut.

beginner: Fast upward growth from a few inches to knee-high and taller, adding leaves and thickening the stalk. Inside, the plant is already forming the tassel and ears, so steady water and feeding at this stage set up your harvest.
seasoned: Rapid upward growth from a few inches to knee-high and beyond, adding leaves and building the stalk that will carry the ears. Reproductive parts (tassel and ears) are being set inside now, so steady water and feeding here shape the crop.

beginner: How tall is your corn getting? Note its height and when you fed it.
seasoned: How is your corn filling in? Note the height, leaf count, and any sidedressing you did.

beginner: Keep the water steady and generous now, because this begins the most important stretch for the crop. Feed once more with nitrogen as the tassels appear, and try not to shake the plants and lose pollen early.
seasoned: Do not let the bed dry out: this is the start of the critical-moisture window. Keep water high and steady, sidedress nitrogen again as tassels emerge, and avoid anything that knocks pollen off prematurely.

beginner: A feathery tassel appears at the very top of each stalk and starts releasing pollen. This is one of the two touchiest weather stages: hot spells over 95°F or dry soil now ruin the pollen and leave you with gappy ears.
seasoned: The tassel pushes out of the top of the stalk and begins shedding pollen. This is one of the two most weather-sensitive stages: heat over 95°F or drought here kills pollen and thins the eventual kernel set.

beginner: Have the tassels come out at the top? Note the date and whether it was hot or dry while they shed pollen.
seasoned: Have the tassels emerged? Note the date and any heat or dry spell during pollen shed.

beginner: Keep the water at its highest and steadiest now, because silking is the stage that suffers most from dry soil. Water deeply through any hot spell, and leave the plants alone while pollen is landing on the fresh silks.
seasoned: Hold moisture at its peak: silking is the single most drought-sensitive stage. Water deeply through any heat wave, and do not disturb the block while pollen is shedding onto the fresh silks.

beginner: Silks come out of the top of each young ear a day or two after the tassels open, and every silk that catches pollen turns into one kernel. The silks can be pollinated for up to two weeks. Silks that dry up without pollen mean empty ears.
seasoned: Silks emerge from the ear tips a couple of days after the tassel opens; each silk that catches pollen becomes one kernel. Silks stay receptive for up to two weeks. Brown, dry silks with no pollination leave blank ears.

beginner: Have the silks appeared at the top of the ears? Note the date, since the corn is usually ready about 18 to 20 days after.

beginner: Brown, papery husks, dead silks, and hard, dented kernels that barely dent when you press them with a thumbnail. Unlike sweet corn, you want the ear fully mature and dry, not green and juicy.
seasoned: Brown, papery husks, dead silks, and hard, dented kernels that barely mark under a thumbnail. Unlike milk-stage sweet corn, the ear is meant to be fully mature and dry, not plump and green.

beginner: Have you picked the dried ears? Note the date and about how many ears you got.

seasoned: Shuck the harvested ears and spread them in a single layer in a warm, dry, airy place to finish drying; a fan speeds it. Once the kernels are hard and glassy (about 13 to 15 percent moisture), shell them off the cobs and store the dry grain, grinding to meal only as needed.

beginner: Kernels that are hard and glassy, do not dent when pressed, and pop off the cob easily. If you smash a few with a hammer and they shatter instead of smearing, they are dry enough to store.
seasoned: Kernels that are hard, glassy, and no longer dent under a thumbnail, and that shell cleanly off the cob. A few kernels smashed with a hammer should shatter rather than smear, the sign they are dry enough to store.

beginner: Have you shelled the corn off the cobs and stored it? Note the date and how the drying went.
seasoned: Have you shelled and stored the grain? Note the date and how the kernels dried down.

seasoned: Keep corn watered through pollination

seasoned: Let your field corn dry down

beginner: Plant corn in a square block of short rows, not one long row. Corn is pollinated by wind, so the pollen from the tassels has to drift down onto the silks. A block of at least four short rows (think four rows of four) keeps the pollen among the plants, so the ears fill out with full kernels.
seasoned: Plant corn in a BLOCK, not a long single row. Corn is wind-pollinated: the tassel sheds pollen that must fall on the silks, and a block of at least four short rows (a 4 by 4 grid) fills the ears far better than one long row where pollen blows off to the side.

beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F before planting. Corn seed rots in cold, wet soil, so planting early just gives you gaps in the stand. There is nothing to gain by rushing.
seasoned: Wait for soil at least 60°F before sowing. Corn seed rots or takes chilling injury in cold, wet ground, and there is no head start to be had from early planting.

beginner: Keep field corn away from sweet corn and popcorn. Its pollen will drift in and spoil them, making sweet corn starchy and stopping popcorn from popping. Keep them at least 300 feet apart, or, since that is a lot of room, plant them so they tassel about two weeks apart instead.
seasoned: Keep field corn away from sweet corn and popcorn: its dent pollen crosses sweet corn to starchy kernels and keeps popcorn from popping. Isolate by at least 300 feet, or, since that is impractical in most home gardens, stagger tasseling by at least two weeks.

beginner: Feed corn with nitrogen when it is about knee-high and again when the tassels appear. Corn is a hungry crop, and those are the two times it needs the most food. In sandy soil, feed a little more often, since the nitrogen washes away.
seasoned: Sidedress nitrogen at knee-high and again as tassels form. Corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder, and the two demand peaks are rapid stalk growth and the run-up to pollination; sandy soils call for splitting it further.

beginner: Keep the soil moist while the tassels are shedding pollen. Hot weather over 95°F or dry soil now ruins the pollen, so the ears end up with missing kernels. Water deeply and keep it steady through this stretch.
seasoned: Do not let the bed dry out at tasseling. Heat over 95°F or drought as pollen sheds kills pollen viability and thins the kernel set. Keep moisture high and steady through the pollination window.

beginner: Silking is the most important time of all for water. If the corn dries out now, the silks cannot catch and hold pollen, and that costs you more than dry weather at any other time. Water deeply through any hot spell while the silks are out.
seasoned: Silking is the single most drought-sensitive stage: stress here desiccates silks and pollen and gives the greatest yield loss of any timing. Water deeply through any heat wave while the silks are receptive.

beginner: Keep watering steadily while the ears fill, then ease off as the crop nears the end. After the corn has been pollinated, dry soil shows up as missing kernels at the tip of the ear, so do not let it dry out until the kernels are full.
seasoned: Hold steady moisture through ear fill, then ease off as the crop nears maturity. Once pollination has succeeded, dry conditions show up as aborted kernels at the ear tip, so keep water even until the kernels are well filled.

beginner: Harvest field corn dry, not green like sweet corn. Wait until the husks are brown and papery and the kernels are hard and dented, then pick the ears and finish drying them indoors before shelling. There is no narrow window to catch, so the timing is easy.
seasoned: Harvest field corn dry, not green. Let the husks turn brown and papery and the kernels harden to a full dent, then pick and finish drying under cover before shelling. Unlike sweet corn there is no 4-to-5-day window, so the timing is forgiving.

beginner: Let field corn dry out on the plant and stop watering once the kernels dent. In dry weather you can leave the ears standing to keep drying on the stalk. In humid weather, watch for mold and be ready to pick them as soon as the kernels are hard.
seasoned: Let field corn dry down on the stalk and stop watering once the kernels dent. The grain matures at black layer (about 30 to 35 percent moisture) and then only loses water. In dry weather leave it standing to field-dry; in humid weather watch for mold and be ready to pick at hard dent.

beginner: After you pick the ears, pull the husks back and spread them out somewhere warm, dry, and airy to finish drying, using a fan to help. Once the kernels are hard and glassy, twist them off the cobs, store the dry grain, and grind it into cornmeal only when you need it.
seasoned: After picking, shuck the ears and spread them in a warm, dry, airy place to finish drying; a fan speeds it. Shell the kernels once they are hard and glassy (about 13 to 15 percent moisture), then store the dry grain and grind to meal only as needed.

beginner: Each plant gives about one or two ears of dry grain. A 10-foot row in your block yields roughly a dozen to two dozen dried ears, which comes to a few pounds of kernels once you shell them off the cobs for grinding.
seasoned: Each stalk yields one to two mature ears of dry grain. Home plantings are measured in ears rather than bushels: a 10-foot block row returns roughly a dozen to two dozen dried ears, which shell out to a few pounds of grain for grinding.

beginner: There is no rush like there is with sweet corn. The whole block dries down together in fall, you bring it in once, and the dry grain keeps for years, so you harvest it all at once instead of checking it every day.
seasoned: Unlike sweet corn there is no fleeting peak. The whole block matures and dries down together over a few weeks in fall, and the dry grain then keeps for years, so the harvest is a single event rather than a race against the milk stage.

beginner: Field corn is not hard to grow, but it needs room and time: a block of several rows and a long, warm season of 95 to 120 days to dry down. The payoff is an easy harvest with no daily checking, and dry grain that stores for years.
seasoned: Field corn is easy to grow but demands space, a long season, and patience: it needs a block of several rows for pollination and a full 95 to 120 days to dry down. Its great advantage over sweet corn is a forgiving, one-shot harvest and grain that stores for years.

beginner: Ears with bare patches and missing kernels
seasoned: Ears with gaps and missing kernels

beginner: The ears came out with bare patches because those silks never got pollinated. This usually happens when the corn was planted in too small a group (a single row or a few plants), or when heat or dry soil during silking ruined the pollen and dried up the silks.
seasoned: The ears filled unevenly with blank patches because pollination failed on those silks. The usual causes are a too-small planting (a single row or a few plants), heat over 95°F or drought during silking that killed pollen and dried the silks, or silks that were never dusted because the block was too sparse.

beginner: Plant a block of at least four short rows so the wind can pollinate well, and keep the water steady while the tassels and silks are out. Try to time it so silking is not in the hottest part of summer, and in a small patch you can gently shake the tassels at midday to spread pollen.
seasoned: Plant a BLOCK of at least four short rows so wind pollination is thorough, and keep moisture high and steady through tasseling and silking. Time plantings so silking misses the worst summer heat, and hand-shake the tassels at midday in a small planting to help.

beginner: Field corn, also called dent corn, is a tall grass grown not for fresh eating but for the hard, dry grain inside the ear. You let the ears ripen and dry right on the stalk, then shell off the kernels to grind into cornmeal, grits, or masa for tortillas, or to feed to livestock and poultry. Old open-pollinated types like John Haulk and Cocke's Prolific can tower up to 15 feet, while modern grain hybrids are shorter and faster. Like all corn it is pollinated by wind, so you plant it in a square block of short rows, not a single line, so the tassels can dust the silks and fill the ears. One important warning: field corn pollen will drift into nearby sweet corn or popcorn and ruin them, turning sweet kernels starchy and keeping popcorn from popping, so keep them at least 300 feet apart or time your plantings so they tassel about two weeks apart.
seasoned: Field corn (Zea mays var. indentata), or dent corn, is a tall, frost-tender warm-season grass grown to full maturity for its hard, starchy grain rather than picked green like sweet corn. The ears dry down on the stalk to a hard, dented kernel, then are shelled and ground into cornmeal, grits, hominy, or masa, or kept as livestock and poultry feed. Representative types run from towering open-pollinated heirlooms (John Haulk, Cocke's Prolific, Reid's Yellow Dent, Bloody Butcher) to compact modern grain hybrids chosen by relative maturity. It is wind-pollinated and block-planted, a heavy nitrogen feeder with the same critical moisture window at tasseling and silking as sweet corn. The one isolation rule that matters: dent pollen crossing into sweet corn turns the kernels starchy, and crossing into popcorn destroys its pop, so isolate by about 300 feet or stagger tasseling by roughly two weeks.

beginner: Field corn is ready to harvest when the whole ear has dried down on the stalk: the husks have turned brown and papery, the silks are long dead, and the kernels are hard and dented, not soft or milky. Press a thumbnail into a kernel and it should barely dent. Unlike sweet corn there is no rush, so in good weather you can leave the ears to dry further on the plant. Then pick them, pull back the husks, and finish drying them indoors before you shell off the kernels.
seasoned: Harvest at full physiological maturity and beyond, when the husks are brown and papery, the kernels are hard and fully dented, and a black layer has formed at the kernel base (about 30 to 35 percent kernel moisture at that point). For storage the grain needs to reach roughly 13 to 15 percent moisture, so leave sound ears to field-dry on the stalk in dry weather, or pick at hard dent and finish drying them under cover. There is no narrow window as with milk-stage sweet corn.

beginner: Pick a sunny spot and mix in compost before planting, because corn is a hungry crop that grows tall. Plant it in a block of at least four short rows rather than one long row: a small square (say four rows of four plants) lets the wind carry pollen from the tassels onto the silks, so the ears fill out with full kernels instead of gappy ones. Keep field corn well away from sweet corn and popcorn, because its pollen will drift in and spoil them.
seasoned: Work compost or aged manure into a full-sun bed before planting; corn is a heavy feeder and roots deeply. Lay the planting out as a BLOCK of at least four short rows (a 4 by 4 grid beats one long row) so wind pollination fills the ears evenly. Keep field corn well away from sweet corn and popcorn, since its dent pollen crosses into them and ruins them, turning sweet corn starchy and keeping popcorn from popping.
